name: Karl Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sell homes at Fairbanks & Rowe, a smart agency in a well-off suburb, mostly four- and five-bedroom houses with gardens and long drives. A normal day is a valuation or two, three viewings and a lot of time on the phone with buyers' lawyers. I use AI all day: it drafts my brochures, sorts my leads, preps my valuation notes and reminds me who to call. I enjoy the deal, the handshake, the moment the numbers finally line up. I don't enjoy waiting six weeks for a slow solicitor.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into using AI so heavily?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I just tried things early and kept what worked. My manager, Phil, was sceptical, then he saw my numbers go up and now he pays for the tools. I'm not a top seller, about average on deals, but I get through more work than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and people who use it do better, which is what I've always said. At work I'd keep showing the others how. Online I'd post about how small business beats hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed. I'd hoped it would let me do the work of three agents. But my job is safe, the pay is good, and I'm set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do, and keep building my tools. I'd keep investing every month in a few index funds and shares, about seven hundred pounds. My girlfriend Hana and I would probably get engaged next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taxes and regulation more than anything. Every year there's a new rule for agents, a new form for landlords. That costs more time than AI saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should fix that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Government should get out of the way, mostly. Fewer forms, lower taxes on small firms. Let people work.

I'd post that **small business** beats hype, and keep showing colleagues how.
think: I'd be a little **disappointed** it didn't do the work of three agents.
My **job and pay** are safe, and I'm set.
do: Keep building **his AI tools** for brochures and leads.
Invest about **£700 a month** in index funds and shares.

fieldNote: His main gripe is **regulation**, not AI.
He is **disappointed** AI didn't do more.
He links his **free-market views** to his hopes for small business and fewer forms.

steps.text: Keep building his AI tools for brochures and leads
Invest about £700 a month in index funds and shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's great for agents who learn it, and I'd say it loudly. At work I'd push everyone to get on board. Online I'd share how I use it, maybe start a small newsletter for agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. I'm already there. The risk is that firms need fewer of us, but I'd be the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Phil to make me the person who sets up the tools for all three Fairbanks & Rowe branches, with a pay rise for it. I'd start thinking about my own small agency, with me plus tools doing what five people do now. And I'd keep investing, maybe a bit more in AI firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Fairbanks & Rowe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a couple of years, maybe. Starting your own agency with AI costs much less than it used to. That's the opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about colleagues who don't learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's their choice. I'd offer to help, and I'd mean it. But I won't carry anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge opportunity and we should embrace it. At work I'd be calm and practical. Online I'd argue against heavy-handed rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's more of a shake-up than I'd like. If AI can value, market and negotiate as well as me by 2028, buyers might skip agents altogether. My own agency plan might not have time to pay off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch my own agency straight away, before the big firms catch up, using every tool I can. I'd move more savings into AI company shares, since that's where the money goes. I'd still keep a year's cash in the bank, because Hana and I want to buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited and nervous. It's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the three years before robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that saves agents for a while. Rich buyers want a person walking them round a five-bedroom house. I'd do that bit myself and let AI do everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a dentist, so she's safe until the robots. She'd say go for it, but keep the savings. She's more careful than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead, if you start now. At work I'd push Phil to modernise all three branches. Online I'd say keep government out of it, because rules written in a panic always land on small firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's ideal for me. I'd have time to build my own agency and get in before the big chains work it out. Robots come about three years after the AI, so viewings stay a human job until around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd marry Hana and we'd buy a house, a three-bed near her practice. I'd start my agency in year two, after building up another few months of savings. I'd use AI for everything except the viewings and the handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, honestly, maybe more than I should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you're wrong about buyers wanting a person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd pivot to helping other agencies set up their AI tools. I've already done it for three branches at Fairbanks & Rowe. Either way, the skills sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why marry in year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want a family, and I'd rather be settled before I take the risk. My parents married at twenty-five and ran a shop together for thirty years. That's the model I grew up with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and the free market will sort most of it out. At work I'd tell Phil this is our chance to become the agency everyone copies. Online I'd push for less regulation on new firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be 37 when it arrives, hopefully with my own agency, a couple of kids and a paid-down mortgage. The robots come at 40, and by then I'd want to be the owner, not the one doing viewings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Hana, buy a house, and start my agency in about three years. I'd keep investing about seven hundred a month. I'd keep learning every new tool the week it comes out, because that's my edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Genuinely calm, which I know is not how most people feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk you're too confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Ten years is long, and plenty can go wrong, like a crash or a bad law. But I'd rather be ready than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger agents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools now and build something. Don't wait for anyone to save you. That's what I tell our junior, Amir, every week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my agency might not have time to pay off. What would help is less red tape for new businesses, so people like me can move fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about people who struggle with change. I'd want people who don't adapt looked after by their families and communities, not just the state. But I know not everyone has a family like mine.

headlineQuote: I'd want people who don't adapt looked after by their families and communities, not just the state.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old sales negotiator** at a premium suburban agency, selling large family houses.
He uses **AI all day** and believes it lifts his work rate above average.
He holds **free-market** views and dislikes regulation.
He stays **calm** in most scenarios, uneasy only when AGI arrives fast, and plans **his own agency**.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, when his own agency might not have time to pay off.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **less red tape** for new businesses.
